front: Scheduling: what is the scheduler's single objective, and from where does it pick?
back: The scheduler decides how and when ready tasks run on the shared CPUs. Its single objective is to pick the next task to run from the ready queue (runqueue). It applies to both user-level and kernel-level tasks.

front: Scheduling: on which events is the scheduler dispatched?
back:
• The CPU becomes idle (e.g. a task issues an I/O request and goes on a wait queue)
  • A timeslice expires
  • A new task becomes ready / enters the runqueue

front: Scheduling: what is the runqueue, and why is its form tied to the policy?
back: The runqueue (ready queue) is the central data structure; it is only logically a queue. Its concrete form is chosen to match the policy because policy and structure are tightly coupled: a structure optimized for one policy is usually a poor fit for another. FCFS needs only the head; SJF must locate the minimum-runtime task, so a sorted structure or tree is preferable.

front: Scheduling: match each policy to its natural runqueue form (FCFS, SJF, Priority, Multi-level feedback, Linux CFS).
back:
• FCFS: simple FIFO queue
  • SJF: ordered queue or balanced tree keyed on run time
  • Priority: a separate runqueue per priority level
  • Multi-level feedback: several queues, each with its own timeslice and rules
  • Linux CFS: red-black tree keyed on virtual runtime

front: Scheduling: list the steps to put a thread on the CPU.
back:
1. The scheduler selects a task from the runqueue according to its policy
  2. The task is dispatched: the OS context switches to it, enters user mode, sets the program counter to the task's next instruction, and execution begins

front: Scheduling overhead: what does timeslicing overhead consist of, and how does it affect the metrics?
back: Timeslicing takes time: the OS must interrupt the running task, run the scheduler, and context switch to the new task. Counting this overhead, total time grows, so throughput goes down; each task starts a little later, so wait and completion times go up.

front: Scheduling: when is a timeslice worthwhile relative to context-switch time?
back: When the timeslice is significantly longer than the context-switch time; then the context-switching overheads are minimized. Even with no other runnable task the timer still fires at each timeslice interval, but with no scheduling or context switching (the dominant part of the overhead) the overhead is much smaller.

front: Scheduling: the frequency tradeoff, short vs. long timeslices?
back: Frequent preemption (short timeslices): lowers wait before first run, more responsive, but multiplies context-switch overhead, lowering throughput and raising average completion time. Infrequent preemption (long timeslices): amortizes overhead, improves throughput and completion time, at the cost of longer waits.

front: Scheduling: which timeslice do CPU-bound tasks prefer, and why?
back: Long (ideally infinite). The user perceives completion, not start, so wait time barely matters. Fewer context switches keep CPU utilization and throughput high. With no preemption at all the metrics are best.

front: Scheduling: which timeslice do I/O-bound tasks prefer, and why?
back: Short. A short quantum lets the task issue its I/O request sooner, then block and yield. This keeps the device busy, hides I/O latency behind other tasks, and keeps user-perceived response time low.

front: Scheduling: why does timeslice length only matter in a mixed CPU/I/O workload, not a pure I/O one?
back: A pure I/O-bound task issues a blocking request every quantum and yields voluntarily before the timeslice expires, so lengthening the timeslice changes nothing. In a mix, a CPU-bound task holding a long timeslice forces a co-resident I/O-bound task to wait for the quantum to expire; its I/O latency can no longer be hidden, device utilization drops, throughput falls, and its wait balloons. That is why a shorter timeslice helps the mixed case.

front: Scheduling metrics: give the formulas for throughput, average completion time, and average wait time (tasks arrive at 0).
back:
• Throughput = number of tasks / total time to finish all tasks
  • Average completion time = mean of (finish_i - arrival_i)
  • Average wait time = mean of (start_i - arrival_i)
Start = first instant on the CPU; finish = completion time.

front: Scheduling metrics: two rules easy to forget when building a timeline?
back:
• Context switching takes time; add it between tasks when preemption actually occurs
  • An I/O-bound task that blocks cannot hide its latency if there is no other runnable task to switch to, so the device service time must be added to the timeline in that case

front: Scheduling worked example (T1=1s, T2=10s, T3=1s, arrive at 0, no switch cost): compute FCFS metrics.
back:
Order T1, T2, T3; finishes at 1, 11, 12.
  • Throughput = 3/12 = 0.25 tasks/s
  • Average completion = (1+11+12)/3 = 8.00 s
  • Average wait = (0+1+11)/3 = 4.00 s

front: Scheduling worked example (T1=1s, T2=10s, T3=1s): compute SJF metrics and compare to FCFS.
back:
Order T1, T3, T2; finishes at 1, 2, 12.
  • Throughput = 3/12 = 0.25 tasks/s (unchanged)
  • Average completion = (1+2+12)/3 = 5.00 s
  • Average wait = (0+1+2)/3 = 1.00 s
SJF improves completion and wait by front-loading short jobs, but assumes run times are known in advance (estimated in practice).

front: Scheduling worked example (T1=1s, T2=10s, T3=1s): round robin, timeslice 1s, compute metrics.
back:
T1 runs 0 to 1 (done); T2 runs 1 to 2 (preempted); T3 runs 2 to 3 (done); T2 resumes 3 to 12 (done).
  • Average completion = (1+12+3)/3 = 5.33 s
  • Average wait = (0+1+2)/3 = 1.00 s
Round robin matches SJF's wait and comes close on completion without needing run-time knowledge.

front: Scheduling worked example (two 10s CPU-bound tasks, switch 0.1s): compare timeslice infinite vs. 1s.
back: Infinite (run to completion): no switch cost; average wait = (0+10)/2 = 5.00 s; average completion = (10+20)/2 = 15.00 s. Timeslice 1s: 20 one-second slices plus 19 switches of 0.1 s, so the total is 21.9 s (T1 ends at 20.8 s, T2 at 21.9 s): throughput 0.091 tasks/s, average wait 0.55 s, average completion 21.35 s (the graphic says 20.85). Smaller timeslices start tasks sooner but degrade throughput and completion, which is why CPU-bound tasks want long timeslices.

front: Scheduling errata: for the 5-second CPU-bound case, what is the corrected average wait and what was wrong?
back: The corrected average wait is 2.55 s, not 3.05 s. The lecture slide contained a division error that the errata corrects.

front: MLFQ: what is the motivation, and why is it more than a stack of priority queues?
back: The scheduler cannot know in advance whether a task is CPU-bound or I/O-bound, and behavior can change over a task's lifetime. The MLFQ holds several queues, each with a different timeslice and its own rules, and learns which queue a task belongs in by observing its behavior. The feedback mechanism is the point, not merely stacked priority queues.

front: MLFQ: why do the top and lower queues have different timeslices?
back:
• Topmost queue, shortest timeslice: suited to I/O-bound tasks, which issue a blocking request and yield quickly, so a short quantum gets them on and off the CPU fast, hiding I/O latency and keeping the device busy
  • Lower queues, longer timeslices: suited to CPU-bound tasks, which are penalized by frequent context switches and benefit from longer uninterrupted runs

front: MLFQ: how do threads move between queues?
back:
• A new task enters at the top (shortest timeslice)
  • If it yields or blocks before its quantum expires, that confirms I/O-bound; it stays at the short-timeslice queue
  • If it uses its entire quantum and is preempted, it is more CPU-bound, so it is pushed down to a longer-timeslice queue
  • If a task in a lower queue starts yielding early due to I/O, the scheduler boosts it back up
The feedback signal is preemption (CPU-bound) vs. voluntary yield (I/O-bound).

front: MLFQ: how many levels does Solaris use?
back: Solaris uses an MLFQ with 60 levels and its own promotion/demotion rules.

front: Linux O(1) scheduler: what does O(1) mean, and how many priority levels does it have?
back: It selects and enqueues a task in constant time regardless of the number of tasks. It is preemptive and priority-based with 140 priority levels: 0 to 99 are real-time; 100 to 139 are timesharing (user tasks default to 120, adjusted by a nice value from -20 to +19).

front: Linux O(1) scheduler: how are timeslices assigned across priorities, and why?
back: The assignment is inverted from the naive intuition: the smallest timeslices go to the lowest-priority (CPU-bound) tasks and the largest to higher-priority interactive tasks. Since low-priority tasks only run after all higher-priority tasks, a small quantum ensures they do not block the important tasks for long once they get the CPU.

front: Linux O(1) scheduler: what is the feedback rule based on, and how are priorities adjusted?
back: The feedback rule is based on sleep time (time idle or waiting). A task that sleeps more is treated as interactive and boosted (priority - 5); a task that sleeps little is treated as compute-bound and penalized (priority + 5).

front: Linux O(1) scheduler: how do the active and expired arrays work?
back:
• The scheduler always picks from the active array, using a bitmask and find-first-set-bit trick to locate the highest-priority non-empty level in constant time
  • A task that yields or is preempted with time left returns to the active array at its level
  • A task that exhausts its entire timeslice moves to the expired array
  • Only when the active array is empty do the two arrays swap

front: Why did the O(1) scheduler give way to CFS?
back: Structural flaw: a task in the expired array cannot run again until every active-array task has exhausted its timeslice, causing unacceptable jitter for latency-sensitive apps (e.g. a Skype call). More broadly, O(1) made no real fairness guarantee (no CPU time in proportion to priority over an interval). These motivated the Completely Fair Scheduler, default for non-real-time tasks since Linux 2.6.23.

front: CFS: what structure and key does it use, and what does vruntime mean?
back: CFS keeps runnable tasks in a red-black tree ordered by vruntime (virtual runtime), the time a task has spent running, tracked to nanosecond granularity. Left nodes have smaller vruntime (more deserving of the CPU); right nodes have larger vruntime.

front: CFS: describe the scheduling algorithm and how priority is encoded.
back:
1. Schedule the leftmost node (least vruntime), found in constant time
  2. Periodically increment the running task's vruntime and compare to the leftmost; if it still has the smallest vruntime it keeps running, else it is preempted and reinserted
  3. Priority is encoded in the rate vruntime advances: fast for low-priority tasks (preempted sooner), slow for high-priority tasks (run longer)

front: CFS: what are the time complexities of selection and insertion, and what limits scaling?
back: Selection is O(1); insertion is O(log n) in the total number of tasks in the system. That log(n) insertion cost is the theoretical limit on scaling CFS to very large task counts.

front: Fedorova: what is the goal of the scheduler she argues for on CMT hardware?
back: On chip multithreading (CMT) hardware where several threads share a core's pipeline, the scheduler should maximize system throughput by managing resource contention, not just balance load. Each hardware context looks like a logical processor; co-scheduled threads compete for the shared pipeline. (Paper, Fedorova et al.: a CMT-aware scheduler can improve application performance by as much as a factor of two over a naive one.)

front: Fedorova: what thread mix is best, and why are two compute-bound or two memory-bound threads bad?
back: The best mix co-schedules threads with complementary resource needs: one compute-bound and one memory-bound keeps both the pipeline and memory system busy. Two compute-bound threads contend for the pipeline (each degrades roughly by half) while memory sits idle; two memory-bound threads leave the pipeline idle while both wait on memory.

front: Fedorova: what is IPC under the lecture's model, and what does it indicate for compute- vs. memory-bound threads?
back: Each thread can issue one instruction per cycle, so per core max IPC is 1 (aggregate 4 across four cores). A compute-bound thread approaches IPC = 1; a memory-bound thread, stalled on memory, has IPC well below 1.

front: Fedorova: what metric does she propose, and what do low and high values mean?
back: She proposes cycles per instruction (CPI), the reciprocal of IPC, as the scheduling signal. A compute-bound thread completes an instruction almost every cycle, so CPI is about 1; a memory-bound thread stalls many cycles per instruction, so CPI is high.

front: Fedorova: the CPI experiment setup and its exam-facing conclusion?
back: A simulator modeled 4 cores with 4 hardware contexts each (16 contexts); a synthetic workload of 16 threads with CPIs of 1, 6, 11, 16 (four of each; CPI 1 most compute-bound, 16 most memory-bound). Four schedules used IPC as the metric. Conclusion: scheduling threads with mixed CPI values yields higher platform utilization; schedules spreading high/low CPI across cores gave high IPC, clustering similar CPI gave low IPC.

front: Fedorova: the exam-facing takeaway after profiling real benchmarks?
back: Real CPI values cluster together rather than spreading out as the synthetic workload did, so CPI by itself may not be an instructive scheduling metric in practice.

front: Fedorova: lecture says Fedorova "speculates" CPI is useful and frames high CPI simply as memory-bound. What does the paper actually say?
back: The paper is more assertive: mean CPI "gives us a useful window into the dynamic instruction mix" and "nicely captures average instruction delay." It reasons through single-threaded CPI (the CPI a thread would show on a dedicated core), where a high value means low pipeline resource demand.

front: Fedorova: lecture calls the simulated platform "4-way SMT." What did the paper actually model?
back: The paper modeled fine-grained multithreading: one set of functional units interleaving threads with a context switch every cycle, at most one instruction issued per cycle, and it explicitly named SMT as the design it did not build. (The course treats SMT, hyperthreading, and CMT as synonyms.)

front: Fedorova: lecture gives a pessimistic "CPI clusters, not instructive" conclusion. What is the paper's own view and stated limitations?
back: The paper is optimistic: measured CPI "can vary by an order of magnitude among applications," near-term CPI is predictable, and a CPI-balancing scheduler "should be a simple matter of engineering." Its stated limitations differ: CPI does not reveal which resource threads contend for (cache hierarchy, FPU), and CPI measured on an already-busy system is perturbed by existing contention. The lecture's skeptical takeaway aligns with Fedorova's later USENIX 2005 work finding L2 cache contention, not pipeline CPI, dominant.

front: Fedorova: which hardware performance counters help classify a thread and judge utilization?
back:
• Instructions retired (from which IPC can be computed): IPC near 1 suggests compute-bound; low IPC / high CPI suggests memory-bound
  • Cache miss counters (L1, L2, LLC): high LLC miss rate suggests memory-bound (or a cold cache after a phase change); few misses suggest compute-bound
  • Power/energy counters: additional input for the scheduler's model
Read via interfaces like oprofile or Linux perf.

front: Fedorova: why doesn't software sleep-time tracking work for classifying threads on CMT hardware?
back: A thread stalled on memory is not sleeping on a software queue, and software accounting is far too slow when a hardware context switch costs only cycles. Schedulers therefore combine several hardware counters, often through platform-specific models trained on known workloads, to pick a thread mix that keeps all components busy with minimal interference.

front: Memory: how does the OS map a process's memory to physical DRAM?
back: Each process gets its own virtual address space, mapped to physical DRAM via per-process page tables. The virtual space is divided into fixed-size pages; physical memory into page frames of the same size. A virtual address splits into a VPN and an offset; the VPN indexes the page table to produce a PFN, and PFN + offset gives the physical address. Equal page and frame sizes mean only the frame base needs translating; the offset carries through.

front: Memory: what hardware performs translation, and what x86 register points to the active page table?
back: The memory management unit (MMU) performs translation on every reference and uses the page table entry's bits to validate it. On x86 the CR3 register points to the active process's page table and is reloaded on every context switch.

front: Memory: what is allocation on first touch?
back: Physical memory is assigned lazily: when a process first accesses a newly allocated virtual region, the OS takes a free frame and creates the page table entry at that moment. Memory that is reserved but never touched costs no physical frames.

front: Memory (demand paging): what happens when a process accesses a page that was swapped out?
back: A swapped-out page has the page table entry's present bit set to 0. A later access makes the MMU raise a page fault, trapping into the kernel. The handler brings the page back into a free frame and re-establishes the mapping (very likely not the same frame as before), then resets the PC to the faulting instruction so the reference re-executes and succeeds.

front: Memory: what happens when a process accesses a page not allocated to it?
back: The MMU raises a fault signaling an illegal access: an attempt to access memory that hasn't been allocated. The CPU places an error code on the kernel stack and traps into the kernel's page fault handler, which decides the action from the error code and the faulting address (stored in CR2 on x86). The error code distinguishes this from a not-present page or a permission violation.

front: Memory: how does copy-on-write (COW) work, e.g. on fork?
back:
1. Instead of copying the parent's address space, the OS points the child's page tables at the same physical frames and marks them read-only for both
  2. While either only reads, they safely share one copy (cheap)
  3. On a write, the MMU traps on the protection fault; the kernel copies that single page into a new frame, updates the writer's entry to the private copy with write permission, and lets the write proceed
Only pages actually written are duplicated. Whether write protection is then removed from the original page depends on how many other processes still share it; if other references remain, it stays protected.

front: Memory: why can a process address more memory than physically available? Give the 32-bit example.
back: A virtual address space can far exceed physical DRAM. On a 32-bit architecture each process addresses 2^32 = 4 GB; with 8 GB RAM, three processes could each ask for 4 GB and together demand far more than exists. Resolved by swapping / demand paging: DRAM holds only the pages in use, the rest live on disk.

front: Memory: what policy guides page replacement, and what two PTE bits inform it?
back: The guiding policy is Least Recently Used (LRU): evict the page not used for the longest time. Two bits: the access (reference) bit approximates recency for LRU; the dirty bit shows whether a page was written since loaded. A clean page can be dropped with no disk write; a dirty page must be written back, so the daemon prefers to evict clean pages.

front: Memory: what triggers page replacement, and what is Linux's default variant?
back: Pages are swapped out when memory usage exceeds a threshold and CPU usage is low enough that the page out daemon does not disrupt applications. Linux by default uses a second chance variant of LRU: it performs two scans before deciding which pages to swap out.

front: TLB: describe the translation path on a hit and a miss.
back: Every virtual address is first presented to the TLB, a small hardware cache of recent translations in the MMU. On a TLB hit the physical address is produced immediately, no page-table walk. On a TLB miss the hardware walks the page table, writes the result into the TLB, then the access proceeds through the TLB.

front: TLB: besides the PFN, what else does a TLB entry carry, and why does that matter?
back: The TLB entry also carries the protection and validity bits, so the MMU can validate the access and raise a fault directly from a TLB hit without touching memory.

front: TLB: why does it matter, in terms of memory accesses saved?
back: A single-level page table needs two memory accesses per reference (page table entry, then data); a four-level table needs four page-table reads before the data read. The TLB collapses that into a single lookup on a hit. Despite being small it hits often because references exhibit strong temporal and spatial locality.

front: TLB: give a typical modern x86 TLB organization.
back: The TLB is split, for example a 64-entry data TLB and a 128-entry instruction TLB per core, backed by a shared 512-entry second-level TLB.

front: Page tables: for an X-bit address with a Y-bit offset, give the general size relationships.
back:
• Addressable space = 2^X bytes
  • Page size = 2^Y bytes (Y-bit offset)
  • Number of VPNs / entries = 2^X / 2^Y = 2^(X-Y)
  • Page table size = 2^(X-Y) × entry size
The top (X - Y) bits form the VPN; a flat table needs one entry per VPN.

front: Page tables: work the 32-bit example with 4 KB pages and 4-byte entries.
back:
X = 32, Y = 12.
  • Addressable space = 2^32 = 4 GB
  • Entries = 2^(32-12) = 2^20 (about one million)
  • Each entry = 4 bytes
  • Page table size = 2^20 × 4 = 4 MB, per process

front: Page tables: how large would a flat 64-bit table be (4 KB pages, 8-byte entries), and why is this a problem?
back: 2^3 × 2^64 / 2^12 = 2^55 bytes, on the order of 32 PB per process. A page table is per-process, and a real process uses only a tiny fraction of its address space, yet a flat table reserves an entry for every VPN. This waste is why flat tables are abandoned for hierarchical ones.

front: Hierarchical page tables: what is the benefit, and what is the tradeoff?
back: A multi-level table maps the address space without an entry for every VPN. Inner tables are created only for regions actually used, so gaps cost nothing (a null directory entry, no inner table). The mapping tracks memory actually used, not the theoretical maximum. Tradeoff: more memory accesses per translation (one per level), higher latency, mitigated by the TLB.

front: Hierarchical page tables: why do more levels help, and where does this matter most?
back: More levels make each inner structure cover a smaller region, so gaps are more likely to align with a structure's granularity and let whole directories go unallocated. This matters most on 64-bit platforms, where address spaces are enormous and sparse, so two, three, and four-level tables keep the structures small.

front: Hierarchical page tables (32-bit, split 12/10/10, offset 10 bits): work the structure sizes.
back:
• Directory holds 2^12 entries, so up to 2^12 inner page tables
  • Each inner page table holds 2^10 entries
  • Each inner entry addresses 2^10 bytes (page size)
  • Each inner page table maps 2^10 × 2^10 = 2^20 bytes = 1 MB
Any unallocated 1 MB-aligned gap needs no inner table.

front: Hierarchical page tables (12-bit addresses, split 2/4/6): show the reduction over a flat table.
back: Pages are 2^6 = 64 bytes. A flat 6-bit-VPN table needs 2^6 = 64 entries. In the two-level scheme each of the 4 outer entries covers 2^(4+6) = 1 KB. For a process using the first 2 KB and the last 1 KB: one outer entry maps an unallocated 1 KB gap (no inner table); the other three inner tables hold 2^4 = 16 entries each = 48 total, a 25% reduction over the flat 64-entry table.

front: Hierarchical page tables: the general procedure for entry counts and coverage per level?
back: For each level, entries = 2^(index bits for that level). The coverage of one entry at a given level = (page size) × the product of the entry counts of all levels below it.

front: Shared memory: what must the OS do so two processes can share memory?
back:
1. Allocate a set of physical frames for the shared region (need not be contiguous)
  2. For each process, install page table entries mapping some range of its virtual addresses onto those same frames
  3. The mapping stays valid until the process detaches, which invalidates those page table entries
Then reads and writes in the range are visible to every attached process with no further OS involvement; system calls are used only in the setup phase.

front: Shared memory: describe the SysV shared memory mechanism and its persistence.
back: The OS maintains shared memory as segments keyed by a system-wide key. Calls: shmget (create/open), ftok (generate the key), shmat (attach), shmdt (detach), shmctl with IPC_RMID (control/destroy). Segments are system-wide persistent: a segment survives detachment and lives until explicitly destroyed or reboot. The OS caps the number and total size of segments.

front: Shared memory: describe the POSIX shared memory mechanism.
back:
It uses files rather than segments: files in the tmpfs filesystem, which is really state in physical memory, so the OS reuses its file data structures to represent the shared pages.
  • shm_open: create/open a region
  • mmap: attach
  • munmap: detach
  • close: the regular close on the file descriptor (the lecture's "shared memory close"; POSIX has no shm_close) only removes the file descriptor from the process
  • shm_unlink: deletes the shared memory data structures and frees the segment
A file descriptor names the region, so no key-generation step is needed.

front: Shared memory: do the sharing processes use the same virtual addresses?
back: No. The virtual addresses in each process that point to the shared physical location do not have to be the same. With shmat the programmer may choose the address via the addr argument; passing NULL lets the OS pick. What matters is the mapping: each process's own page tables resolve some range of its virtual addresses to the same physical frames.

front: Shared-memory IPC: is copying eliminated?
back: Reduced but not necessarily eliminated. Data is visible to a peer only if it physically resides in the shared region. If a process produces data elsewhere, it must copy it into the region first, and the peer may copy it back out. The copy is avoided only when a process allocates and operates on data in place within the region. One saved case: if a process only needs to read arguments left in the region, it works on them in place.

front: IPC: contrast the cost structure of message-based copy vs. shared-memory map.
back: Message passing pays a recurring per-message tax: copy from sender into the kernel channel, then into the receiver, with a user/kernel crossing each way; a request-response costs 4 crossings and 4 copies, scaling with data size. Shared memory pays a large but one-time mapping cost, then no user/kernel crossings per operation, with copies only if data is not allocated in the region. If the channel is set up once and used many times it gives a good payoff; even one-time use can perform well, because for a large transfer the copy time of message-based IPC can greatly exceed the map cost.

front: IPC: how does Windows LPC exploit the copy-vs-map crossover?
back: Windows Local Procedure Calls (LPC): payloads below a size threshold are copied through a port-like channel, while larger payloads are copied once into a page-aligned area that is then mapped into the target's address space.

front: Message-based IPC: pros and cons?
back: Pro: relative simplicity; the OS kernel takes care of channel management and synchronization, and processes just send and receive. Con: overhead; every operation is a system call with a copy, so a request-response costs 4 crossings and 4 copies.

front: Message-based IPC: name the three forms and their key properties.
back:
• Pipes: byte stream, two endpoints, no message boundaries
  • Message queues: OS understands discrete, possibly prioritized messages
  • Sockets: send/recv through a kernel buffer, works within a host or across the network

front: Shared-memory IPC: pros and cons?
back: Pro: low per-operation cost once established; the kernel is out of the data path (no per-operation syscalls or kernel copies). Cons: the developer must handle synchronization (concurrent access needs coordination), the communication protocol, and region management (segment count/size, oversized messages).

front: IPC rule of thumb: when prefer message passing vs. shared memory?
back: It depends. Prefer message passing for small or one-off exchanges, where the large one-time mapping cost would not pay off. Prefer shared memory when the channel is set up once and used many times, or when a single large transfer makes the copy cost of message passing exceed the map cost.

front: Inter-process synchronization: what two capabilities must any mechanism provide?
back:
• Coordinating how many processes access the region concurrently (the role a mutex plays)
  • Signaling when data is ready to be consumed (the role condition variables and signals play)
Data in shared memory is concurrently accessible, so the same races as among threads arise and accesses must be synchronized.

front: Inter-process synchronization (threading-library option): pthreads primitives marked process-shared, what two requirements?
back:
• Initialize the primitive with the PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED attribute (set pshared on the attribute struct before init); otherwise it is private to the creating process
  • The synchronization variable itself must live in the shared memory region
Caveat: PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED is not necessarily supported on every platform, which is why OS-provided mechanisms matter.

front: Inter-process synchronization (OS-provided): how does a binary semaphore work across processes?
back: A binary semaphore has states 0 and 1. A process arriving at value 1 decrements it to 0 and proceeds, equivalent to acquiring a lock; a process arriving at 0 blocks. SysV provides a semaphore API similar in form to its shared memory API, and POSIX equivalents exist.

front: Inter-process synchronization (OS-provided): how can message queues coordinate shared-memory access?
back: Implement mutual exclusion via send/recv: e.g. process A writes data to shared memory and sends a "ready" message into the queue; B receives it, reads the data, and sends an "ok" message back. On Linux the SysV calls are msgget, msgsnd, msgrcv, msgctl.

front: Synchronization: why does a lock operation need a hardware atomic instruction?
back: A lock must check whether it is free and, if so, set it busy. In ordinary instructions this is a read-modify-write spanning multiple cycles, and the check and set are distinct in time. Between a thread observing free and writing busy, another thread can observe the same free value and also proceed, so two threads believe they hold the lock. A single hardware instruction performs check-and-set as one indivisible step.

front: Synchronization: what two guarantees does the hardware give an atomic instruction?
back:
• Atomicity: the operation happens completely or not at all; no other operation interleaves between its read and write
  • Mutual exclusion at the hardware level: cores cannot execute the atomic on the same location in parallel; concurrent attempts are serialized by the memory system

front: Synchronization: how does test_and_set make a spinlock correct?
back: The first thread calls test_and_set on a lock valued 0; the instruction atomically sets it to 1 (busy) and returns the old value 0, so it proceeds. Every later thread calls test_and_set, sees it already set, gets 1 back and spins (each such call sets the lock to 1 again, which is harmless because it is already busy). Only one thread wins because only one atomic executes against the location at a time.

front: Synchronization: name three example atomic instructions and what each does.
back:
• test_and_set: atomically read the old value and set the location to 1 (busy); the most widely available
  • read_and_increment: atomically read the current value and increment it; the queueing lock relies on it
  • compare_and_swap

front: Synchronization: why does software built on a specific atomic have to be ported?
back: Which atomics a platform offers, and how efficiently each runs, varies by hardware. Software built on a specific atomic therefore has to be ported to use an atomic the target supports, ideally the most efficient one available there.

front: Spinlocks: why are they useful? (two reasons)
back:
• Simplicity: among the simplest primitives; a failed acquire just spins, repeatedly checking the lock
  • Foundational: because of that simplicity, a basic building block for more complex synchronization constructs

front: Spinlock vs. mutex: what does a waiter do, and the cost of waiting?
back: Spinlock: the waiter is not blocked; it spins on the CPU, burning cycles repeatedly checking the lock until it is free or the thread is preempted. Mutex: the waiter relinquishes the CPU and allows another thread to run. Cost of waiting: spinning wastes CPU cycles on the checking; a blocked waiter may lose performance to cache effects when it is signaled to come back and run.

front: Higher-level sync constructs: what makes them more powerful than mutexes and condition variables?
back: Expressiveness and the reduced opportunity for error that comes with it. Mutexes/CVs are low-level and correct but awkward and error-prone to use directly.

front: Sync: what are the two limits of plain mutexes and condition variables?
back:
• Limited expressive power: arbitrary synchronization conditions are hard to express; the readers/writer problem needed helper variables for its invariants, and priority restrictions need helper variables too, because mutexes and condition variables cannot express priority
  • Easy to misuse: easy to lock/unlock the wrong mutex or signal the wrong CV; mistakes compile fine, and every lock/unlock/wait/signal is a chance for a bug

front: Sync: why is a reader/writer lock more powerful?
back: A reader/writer (shared/exclusive) lock lets the developer declare only the kind of access intended, read or write, and the lock enforces the policy behind the scenes (readers share, writers exclusive). The developer no longer hand-builds and hand-maintains helper variables, so semantics are expressed directly with less room for error.

front: Sync: why is a monitor more powerful, and where did monitors appear?
back: A monitor bundles a shared resource, the entry procedures that access it, and condition variables. Locking/checking happen automatically on entry and unlocking/signaling on exit, hidden from the programmer, removing the most error-prone step. Monitors appeared in the Mesa runtime at Xerox PARC; Java provides them via per-object locks and synchronized methods (the one still-explicit operation is notify).

front: Sync: name other higher-level constructs in the same spirit as reader/writer locks and monitors.
back:
• Serializers (hide explicit signaling, make priorities easy)
  • Path expressions (a regular expression describing legal operation interleavings)
  • Barriers and rendezvous points (block until n threads arrive)
  • Wait-free constructs such as read-copy-update (RCU) that avoid explicit locking
All ultimately rest on hardware atomics.

front: Anderson spinlocks: name the three performance metrics that drive the evolution.
back:
• Latency: time to acquire a free lock (best is a single atomic)
  • Delay (waiting time): time between a lock being released and a waiter acquiring it
  • Contention: traffic on the shared bus/interconnect from atomics and cache-coherence; it slows every CPU's memory access and the lock's own acquire/release

front: Anderson spinlocks: what background about atomics and coherence drives the contention behavior?
back: Atomic instructions bypass the cache and go to the memory controller, and executing an atomic triggers cache-coherence traffic (invalidate or update) across all cached copies regardless of whether the value changed. Under write-invalidate coherence, every atomic forces other spinners to miss and re-fetch.

front: Anderson spinlocks: lecture says atomics "always bypass the cache." What does the paper say?
back: The paper calls that a teaching simplification: real implementations cooperate with the cache, for example taking the dirty value from the holding cache under write-back invalidation. What is genuinely unavoidable is the arbitration and the coherence traffic, with the invalidation happening before the instruction executes even if the value does not change.

front: Anderson Stage 1 (test-and-set): rate its latency, delay, and contention.
back: Every spin iteration executes the atomic. Latency: optimal (a single atomic). Delay: can perform well (the very next test_and_set after a release detects and acquires it). Contention: poor, because every spinning processor goes to memory on each atomic, delaying all other CPUs that need memory.

front: Anderson Stage 2 (test-and-test-and-set): what is the idea, and whom does the paper attribute it to?
back: Separate the test from the atomic: first read the lock's cached copy, and with short-circuit evaluation run test_and_set only when the cached read shows it free. While the lock stays busy, spinners loop on their local caches without touching memory. The paper attributes this to Segall and Rudolph, not Anderson.

front: Anderson Stage 2 (test-and-test-and-set): how are its latency and delay, and how does contention depend on the coherence strategy?
back:
Latency and delay: okay, slightly worse than test-and-set because of the extra step. Contention:
  • No cache coherence (NCC): no improvement; every reference goes to memory
  • Write-update: improved (spinners read updated cached values), but when freed all processors see it free at once and all rush to atomic
  • Write-invalidate: terrible; every attempt to acquire the lock generates contention for the memory module and invalidation traffic

front: Anderson Stage 2: the lecture describes what happens on release. How does the paper frame it?
back: The paper's claim is a transient one: a "quiesce" period after each release during which some processors have pending read misses and others pending doomed test-and-sets, each failing one re-invalidating every copy. For a short critical section this transient dominates, so spin-on-read "has almost as much effect on busy processors as spinning directly on a test-and-set"; the paper measured time-to-quiesce growing linearly with the number of spinners.

front: Anderson Stage 3 (delay-based): what does the delay accomplish, and rate its three metrics.
back: A spinner waits before attempting the atomic, so by the time its delay expires another thread may have taken the lock; it re-checks and only issues the atomic if still free, so fewer doomed atomics fire. Latency: okay. Delay: worse (a thread that sees the lock free must wait; pure waste under no contention). Contention: much improved, because atomics are spread out in time.

front: Anderson Stage 3: delay-after-each-reference vs. delay-after-noticing-free, benefit and cost?
back: Delaying on every reference works even on NCC architectures (every reference goes to memory anyway) by cutting how often a spinner references memory. Cost: it hurts delay even more, and the delay grows with the length of the critical section, so a long critical section inflates every spinner's delay even when contention has not risen.

front: Anderson Stage 3: static vs. dynamic delay, pros and cons?
back: Static delay: a fixed value (e.g. from CPU id), combined with the critical-section length (one process waits 1x the critical section, another 2x, and so on). Simple; spreads atomics well under heavy load, but imposes pointless waits under light load (a high-id CPU may wait long with no contention). Dynamic delay: each thread picks a random delay from a range that grows with perceived contention (counting failed test_and_set operations). Adapts to actual load, avoiding needless waits under light load.

front: Anderson Stage 3: the paper notes the delay schemes are borrowed from network arbitration. What is the analogy, and its caveat?
back: The paper models a lock as a CSMA network: static slots come from BRAM and static delays between references from Aloha; dynamic backoff from Ethernet's exponential backoff, which doubles mean delay per collision, caps it at the number of processors, and restarts each visit at half the previous delay. Caveat: the analogy is imperfect, because a network collision aborts all parties equally while a test-and-set "collision" still lets one processor win.

front: Anderson Stage 4 (queueing / array lock): what is the core idea?
back: Instead of letting all spinners share one lock variable and see the release at once, give each waiter its own location to spin on, and have the releaser signal exactly one successor. On arrival a thread atomically fetches a ticket (its position) via read_and_increment and advances queuelast; it spins while its own flag reads must_wait; to release, the holder resets its own flag to must_wait and sets the next one, flags[(myplace+1) mod p], to has_lock.

front: Anderson Stage 4 (queueing lock): rate latency, delay, and contention.
back: Latency: not very efficient (read_and_increment takes more cycles than test_and_set, plus the modular index computation). Delay: good (each holder directly signals the next element in the queue). Contention: much better than any other lock; the atomic executes once up front, not in the spin loop, and the atomic and the spinning involve separate variables, so invalidation of the atomic variable does not affect spinning.

front: Anderson Stage 4 (queueing lock): what conditions are required for its contention win, and what does it cost?
back: Conditions: the architecture must be cache coherent (else spinning on a flag means remote references), and each flag must sit on its own cache line (else writing one flag invalidates the whole line). Costs: needs read_and_increment (less common than test_and_set) and uses O(n) space (one slot per processor) where other locks need a single location.

front: Anderson queueing lock: what caveats does the paper note that the lecture leaves out?
back:
• It makes the preemption problem worse: if a queued spinner is preempted, every thread behind it waits when it reaches the front until it is rescheduled, forcing lock-step for small frequent critical sections
  • It makes waiting on several locks at once hard (a thread can be in only one queue)
  • Devised independently by Graunke at Sequent
  • On the Sequent Symmetry (atomic increment but no read-and-increment returning the old value), Anderson's measured queueing lock had to protect its sequence number with a separate backoff lock

front: Anderson spinlock summary: rank the four locks on contention, and why can't test-and-test-and-set be placed strictly above test-and-set?
back:
• Queueing: best; atomic once up front, each thread spins on its own location
  • Delay: much improved; spreads out atomics
  • Test-and-test-and-set: depends on coherence: NCC no better than test-and-set, write-update improved, write-invalidate terrible (and the worst lock under load on the write-invalidate Symmetry)
  • Test-and-set: poor; every spinner issues an atomic every iteration

front: Anderson empirical results (Sequent Symmetry, 20 processors, write-invalidate): behavior under high load?
back: The queueing lock performs best and is most scalable: as more processors and load are added, it performs best. Test-and-test-and-set performs worst, because write-invalidate forces on the order of N^2 memory references per release. Among delay locks, static beats dynamic slightly, and delaying after each reference is slightly better than after each release.

front: Anderson empirical results: behavior under light load?
back: Test-and-test-and-set does well thanks to its low latency; dynamic delay beats static (static imposes needless large delays at low contention); the queueing lock does worst, because of its higher latency (complex atomic plus extra per-acquire work).

front: Anderson results: lecture names the queueing lock the sole winner under contention. What does the paper actually conclude?
back: The paper names two joint winners: backoff and queueing both scale well, with backoff better under no contention (lower latency) and queueing better when there are waiting processors (it parallelizes the handoff by doing the atomic's work before the lock is released). The N^2 figure is the lecture's/course quiz's accounting; the paper states the cascade in prose and notes fixing any single cause still leaves bus activity growing linearly with processors.

front: Device I/O: what three groups of control registers does a device expose, and what is each for?
back:
• Command registers: the CPU writes these to tell the device what to do
  • Data registers: used to move data into and out of the device
  • Status registers: the CPU reads these to learn what the device is doing
Inside the device: a microcontroller, on-device memory, and device-specific logic (e.g. chips converting analog to digital signals, or chips to interact with the physical network medium).

front: Device I/O: what are the two ways the CPU reaches device registers?
back:
• Memory-mapped I/O: device registers appear at specific physical memory addresses; the integrated PCI controller routes accesses in that range to the device. The range is set by Base Address Registers (BARs), configured at boot per the PCI protocol
  • I/O port model: x86 in/out instructions name an I/O port and a value: the value written out to the device or read from it

front: Device I/O: list the general steps in sending a command to a device.
back:
1. A user process issues a system call for the operation
  2. The kernel runs the in-kernel stack and preprocesses the buffer into what the device expects (e.g. forming a TCP/IP packet)
  3. The kernel invokes the appropriate device driver
  4. The driver configures the request via PIO or DMA, writing commands into command registers and arranging for data to reach the device
  5. The device performs the request (NIC puts packet on the wire; disk performs the block read)
The driver ensures commands/data are neither overwritten nor dropped before the device consumes them.

front: Device I/O: how does a device signal it has something for the CPU, interrupts vs. polling tradeoffs?
back: Interrupts: the device can raise one as soon as it has information for the CPU; the downside is the handler: its steps cost CPU cycles, interrupt masks may be set/reset, and there are indirect effects from cache pollution. Polling: the OS reads status registers at times of its choosing, e.g. when cache pollution will be lowest, but this adds delay in observing the event, and too much polling adds CPU overhead. The receive path is device -> driver -> kernel -> user process.

front: Device I/O: what is OS bypass?
back: The OS maps a device's registers directly into a user process at setup time, then gets out of the way. The process uses a user-level driver (a manufacturer library) to talk to the device directly, with no kernel on the data path. The OS keeps coarse-grained control (enable/disable, permissions), and because the kernel no longer sits in the middle, the device itself must demultiplex incoming data to the right process.

front: PIO vs. DMA: who moves the data, extra hardware, and best transfer size for each?
back: PIO: no extra hardware; the CPU writes every chunk into the data registers; best for small transfers. DMA: requires a DMA controller that moves data between memory and device; the CPU does one command write plus one DMA configuration step; best for large transfers; the buffer must be pinned (non-swappable) for the whole transfer.

front: PIO vs. DMA worked example: transmit a 1500-byte packet with 8-byte data registers. Count the CPU accesses for each.
back:
• PIO: 1 command-register access + ceil(1500/8) = 188 data-register writes = 189 CPU accesses
  • DMA: 1 command-register access + 1 DMA configuration operation (buffer address and size)

front: PIO vs. DMA: why isn't DMA always better, and where is the crossover?
back: Configuring the controller takes many more cycles than a single memory access, so there is a crossover point. For a device moving little data per operation (a keyboard keystroke), PIO wins because one or two stores beat configuring the controller. For a NIC it depends on transfer size: below the size where stores exceed DMA config cost, PIO wins; past it, DMA wins. Pinning follows from the controller having access only to physical memory.

front: Block device stack: name the layers from application down to device, and where does the VFS go?
back:
1. Application (file interface, POSIX API)
  2. Filesystem: finds the file, checks access, determines which portion to access
  3. Generic block layer: a standard interface to all block devices, giving the filesystem one consistent block API
  4. Device driver
  5. Block device
The filesystem gives user processes a consistent file API; the OS gives the filesystem a consistent block API. The VFS (next section) sits above the filesystems, hiding which underlying filesystem is in use.

front: VFS abstractions: what is an inode, and is it persisted?
back: An inode ("index node") holds the index of all data blocks for one file plus metadata (owner, permissions, size), letting a file's blocks be scattered across the disk. It is persisted, in a block.

front: VFS abstractions: what is a dentry, where is it cached, and is it persisted?
back: A dentry (directory entry) represents one path component during traversal; for /users/ada there is one each for /, /users, /users/ada. It is cached in the dentry cache so repeat lookups skip re-reading directory files. It is not persisted (memory only).

front: VFS abstractions: what is the superblock?
back: The superblock describes how the filesystem is laid out on the device (map of inodes, data blocks, free space) and is used for allocation and lookup. It is persisted.

front: ext2 on disk: what is reserved first, and what does a block group contain?
back: The first block of an ext2 partition is not used by Linux and is often used to boot the system. The rest is divided into block groups (whose size is unrelated to disk geometry). Each holds a super block, a group descriptor (location of the bitmaps, free-inode count, directory count), bitmaps to find free inodes and blocks, the inodes (each a 128-byte structure describing exactly one file), and finally the data blocks.

front: ext2 addressing: with a 128-byte inode and 4-byte block pointers over 1 KB blocks, what is the max file size using direct pointers only?
back: The inode holds at most 32 pointers: 32 × 1 KB = 32 KB maximum file size. That is too restrictive, which motivates indirect pointers.

front: ext2 addressing: with 1 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers (256 pointers/block), what do single, double, and triple indirect pointers address?
back:
256 pointers per block.
  • Single indirect: 256 × 1 KB = 256 KB
  • Double indirect: 256 × 256 × 1 KB = 64 MB
  • Triple indirect: 256 × 256 × 256 × 1 KB = 16 GB

front: ext2 addressing: the classic Linux inode layout and its max file size (4-byte pointers, 1 KB blocks)?
back: 12 direct pointers plus one single, one double, and one triple indirect pointer. Max file size = (12 + 256 + 256^2 + 256^3) × 1 KB ≈ 16 GB.

front: ext2 addressing: moving to 8 KB blocks, what is the max file size, and why does block size amplify disproportionately?
back: 8 KB blocks hold 2048 pointers: max = (12 + 2048 + 2048^2 + 2048^3) × 8 KB ≈ 64 TB. An eightfold block-size increase raises the ceiling far more than eightfold, because the gain compounds through each indirect level.

front: ext2 addressing: the tradeoff of indirect pointers, in disk accesses?
back: Indirect pointers keep the inode small while addressing large files, but cost extra disk accesses. With no indirection, reading a block is at most two accesses (inode, then block). A double-indirect block costs four (inode, two levels of pointer blocks, then the data block).

front: VFS optimizations: what does the buffer cache do and how does it change device access?
back: It keeps blocks in main memory, serving reads and absorbing writes there, flushing to disk only periodically (fsync forces it). It cuts the number of disk accesses; one physical write is amortized across the many writes that hit the cache in between.

front: VFS optimizations: what does I/O scheduling do and how does it change device access?
back: It reorders queued requests so the head services them in a sweep instead of backtracking, reducing head movement (turning random access toward sequential). Example: head at position 15, requests for 25 then 17 arrive; the scheduler writes 17 on the way to 25 rather than overshooting and backtracking.

front: VFS optimizations: what does prefetching do and how does it change device access?
back: On a request for block N it also reads the next few logical blocks into the cache. It trades extra disk bandwidth now for fewer future accesses, relying on spatial locality so later reads become cache hits. Example: reading 17 also pulls in 18 and 19.

front: VFS optimizations: what does journaling do and how does it change device access?
back: It writes a description of each update (block, offset, content) to a log instead of the proper disk location, avoiding many random disk accesses; logged writes are periodically applied to their proper locations. It addresses the risk that data held in memory for the I/O scheduler is lost on a crash. ext3/ext4 use this.

front: VFS optimizations: summarize how each of the four reduces file access overhead.
back:
• Buffer caching: fewer disk accesses; periodic flushes amortize one disk write over many cached writes
  • I/O scheduling: reorders requests to reduce disk head movement, maximizing sequential over random access
  • Prefetching: uses more disk bandwidth to raise the cache hit rate, reducing access latency
  • Journaling: writes update descriptions to a log instead of random disk locations, so buffered data is not lost on a crash

front: Virtualization: define it, and name the components (VM/guest, VMM/hypervisor).
back: Virtualization lets multiple operating systems run concurrently on one physical platform, each under the illusion it owns the hardware. Each OS plus its applications and virtual resources is a virtual machine (VM), also called a guest or domain. Coordination, allocation, and isolation are provided by the virtual machine monitor (VMM), also called the hypervisor.

front: Virtualization: what are the VMM's three responsibilities in the lecture's framing?
back:
• Fidelity: the environment presented to the guest is essentially identical to a real machine (same CPU type, same device types); capacity may differ
  • Performance: guest code runs at worst with minor slowdown; near-native speed
  • Safety/isolation: the VMM is in complete control of resources and keeps VMs from interfering
Popek and Goldberg's definition: a VM is "an efficient, isolated duplicate of the real machine."

front: Virtualization: lecture names fidelity/performance/safety. What does Popek & Goldberg 1974 name and define?
back: The paper names equivalence, efficiency, and resource control. Equivalence: any program has an effect identical to running on the bare machine, with two allowed exceptions, timing differences and reduced resource availability. Efficiency: a statistically dominant subset of instructions executes directly on the real processor with no VMM intervention, which formally excludes pure emulators/interpreters. Resource control: a program cannot touch unallocated resources and under certain circumstances the VMM can regain control of resources already allocated. Equivalence distinguishes a VMM from a time-sharing OS and from plain virtual memory.

front: Virtualization history: why did it start, lapse, and return?
back: Began in the 1960s at IBM, to run diverse workloads under different OSes concurrently on shared mainframes. It lapsed because mainframes were not ubiquitous and other hardware was cheap: most companies ran commodity x86 servers, and it was simpler to buy another machine than to make several OSes coexist. It returned when data centers grew too large, servers sat underutilized (~10 to 20% average), admin headcount and power/cooling bills rose, and companies spent on the order of 70% of IT budget on operating expenses; consolidation brings those costs down.

front: Virtualization history: how does Rosenblum & Garfinkel 2005 sharpen the lecture's "cheap hardware then sprawl" arc?
back: The paper notes the irony that the same combination that killed VMMs, cheap hardware plus capable OSes, later caused the problems VMMs solve: cheap hardware proliferated underused machines, and more capable OSes grew "fragile and vulnerable," pushing admins to one-application-per-machine. It argues a VMM is "less a vehicle for multitasking and more a solution for security and reliability."

front: Virtualization: list the benefits that follow from decoupling OS and apps from the box.
back:
• Consolidation (fewer machines, less space, fewer admins, smaller electric bills)
  • Easier migration (copy and clone onto multiple machines)
  • Availability/reliability (create more VMs as load rises; migrate VMs off a node that is getting hot and likely to fail)
  • Containment of bugs and malicious code in isolated VMs
  • A fertile ground for OS research
  • Affordable legacy-OS support

front: Virtualization: contrast bare-metal (type 1) vs. hosted (type 2) on where the VMM runs and how it handles drivers.
back: Bare-metal (type 1): the VMM runs directly on hardware; it must manage all devices, so a privileged service VM running a standard OS typically runs the drivers (Xen: dom0 runs drivers, guest domUs on top; also VMware ESX). Hosted (type 2): the VMM runs as a module inside a full host OS, reusing the host's existing drivers and services (KVM in Linux plus QEMU). Bare-metal's main difficulty is device non-uniformity; hosted leverages the host but pays host-crossing overhead on I/O.

front: Virtualization: lecture's hosted example is KVM/QEMU. What does Rosenblum & Garfinkel use, and what is its I/O path?
back: The paper uses VMware Workstation as the canonical hosted architecture (the term comes from its reference on VMware Workstation's hosted VMM, Sugerman et al.). Its I/O path: a guest disk read/write becomes a host-OS file read/write, and the guest display renders into a host window. Three advantages: the VMM installs like an ordinary application, inherits the host's rich x86 driver support, and reuses the host's scheduling and resource management. Two disadvantages: high I/O overhead because every request crosses into the host and traverses its layers, and the host OS's lack of resource-management support for performance isolation and service guarantees; together they are why ESX Server dropped the host OS.

front: Virtualization: what is paravirtualization, and why is it useful?
back: The guest OS knows it is virtualized. Instead of issuing operations that fail on virtualized hardware, it makes explicit hypercalls to the hypervisor (like system calls: trap in, perform the operation, return control). This sidesteps the non-virtualizable-instruction problem and reduces full-virtualization overheads (e.g. batched page-table updates). Cost: the guest OS must be modified, so no unmodified or legacy OSes. The lecture attributes this to Xen.

front: Virtualization: lecture's paravirtualization example is Xen. What is the paper's canonical example, and how does the paper frame paravirtualization?
back: The paper's canonical example is Disco, a VMM for the non-virtualizable MIPS architecture (it never mentions Xen). Disco replaced the troublesome instructions with accesses to a special memory location, which also removed the traps and improved performance. The paper frames paravirtualization generally as the VMM builder replacing the non-virtualizable parts of the instruction set with easily virtualized equivalents, so most apps run unmodified while the OS is ported. Its stated drawback is incompatibility (needs vendor cooperation, no legacy OSes, no easy migration), which is why VMware needed binary translation instead.

front: x86 virtualization: what was the core problem on pre-2005 x86?
back: Trap-and-emulate needs every instruction the VMM must mediate to trap when the guest runs it de-privileged. On pre-2005 x86 there were 17 instructions that read or modified privileged state yet did not trap when issued unprivileged. The de-privileged guest OS would issue one, it would not trap, the hypervisor never saw it, and the failure was silent, so the guest carried on with wrong state.

front: x86 virtualization: the lecture's canonical example of a non-trapping instruction?
back: Interrupt enable/disable via the flags register. POPF/PUSHF manipulate the interrupt flag, but issued unprivileged they silently ignore the change to that flag. The hypervisor is never notified the guest wanted to change interrupt status, and the guest never learns the change did not take effect.

front: x86 virtualization: the lecture calls the 17 "privileged but did not trap." Why is that terminology wrong, and what is accurate?
back: Under Popek & Goldberg a privileged instruction is defined as one that traps in user mode, so "privileged but did not trap" is self-contradictory. The accurate statement: the 17 are sensitive but not privileged, they touch privileged state (sensitive) yet do not trap outside ring 0 (not privileged), exactly violating the subset condition. The number 17 is not from Popek & Goldberg; it comes from Robin & Irvine, USENIX Security 2000, who analyzed the ~250 Pentium instructions.

front: x86 virtualization: Popek & Goldberg's definitions of privileged, sensitive, and innocuous instructions, and Theorem 1?
back: Privileged: traps in user mode but not supervisor mode. Sensitive: either control sensitive (changes resources or processor mode outside the memory-trap sequence) or behavior sensitive (result depends on real-memory location or processor mode). Innocuous: otherwise. Theorem 1: a VMM can be constructed for a conventional third-generation machine if the set of sensitive instructions is a subset of the privileged instructions, because then every instruction the VMM must mediate traps. Pre-2005 x86 violated this; the 17 were the counterexamples.

front: x86 virtualization: the two concrete x86 examples Rosenblum & Garfinkel give behind the problem?
back: First, POPF sets/clears the interrupt-disable flag but does not trap unprivileged; it silently drops the change. Second, unprivileged instructions can read privileged state: a guest can read the code-segment register to see the real current privilege level, and because the read does not trap, the VMM cannot patch the value, so the guest sees the physical privilege level instead of its virtual one.

front: x86 protection: how did it used to work (rings), and how were guests arranged for virtualization?
back: x86 had a single mode with four rings: ring 0 most privileged (native OS), ring 3 least (applications). Virtualization software ran the hypervisor in ring 0 and de-privileged the guest OS into ring 1, with guest applications still in ring 3. The last two of four requirements (keep guest-OS-from-application protection; protect the VMM from guest OSes) mean guest OS and VMM cannot share a protection level, so one faulty guest cannot take down the hypervisor.

front: x86 protection: how does it work now (root/non-root modes, VMExit/VMEntry)?
back: Recent x86 adds two protection modes, root and non-root (host and guest), with the four rings in each. The hypervisor runs in ring 0 of root mode; a guest runs in non-root mode with its OS back in ring 0 (of non-root) and apps in ring 3. A guest privileged operation causes a VMExit, trapping to root mode and the hypervisor; when done the hypervisor does a VMEntry back to non-root. The guest OS no longer has to be squeezed into ring 1.

front: x86 virtualization fix 1: how does binary translation (full virtualization, VMware) work?
back: Keep the guest unmodified by inspecting kernel instruction blocks at runtime (at a basic-block granularity, such as a loop or a function) before they execute. A block with none of the 17 instructions is marked safe and runs at hardware speed; a block containing one has that instruction rewritten into an alternate sequence emulating the intended behavior. Overheads are reduced by caching translated fragments and translating only kernel code. Runs unmodified and legacy guests, but adds translation latency.

front: x86 virtualization: what extra detail does Rosenblum & Garfinkel give on VMware's binary translation?
back: VMware runs only kernel code under the translator, translates each block into a similar block with the problematic instructions replaced, and caches it in a trace cache so a block is translated only on first execution. The output "looks much like" paravirtualized output, except changes apply at first execution rather than to OS source. The translator is simpler than cross-ISA translators because source and target ISAs are nearly identical. It is also a performance optimization: removing frequently-trapping privileged instructions cuts trap overhead (high on deep-pipeline x86), and once the trace cache is warm, speed is nearly indistinguishable from direct execution.

front: x86 virtualization fix 2: how does paravirtualization (Xen) address the 17 non-trapping instructions?
back: It is the second way to deal with them (after binary translation). Rather than rewriting the guest binary at runtime, the guest OS is modified so it knows it is virtualized and does not issue the problematic instructions (e.g. POPF from ring 1); instead it packages its context and makes explicit hypercalls to the hypervisor. It gives up unmodified/legacy guests in exchange for performance.

front: x86 virtualization fix 3: how did hardware virtualization (around 2005, AMD Pacifica / Intel Vanderpool) fix the problem?
back: The chips were changed so the 17 instructions trap and pass control to the hypervisor, and the root/non-root modes were added. Per-vCPU state lives in a hardware-walked control structure (VMCS on Intel, VMCB on AMD) specifying what traps. Memory structures were tagged with VM identifiers, enabling extended page tables and tagged TLBs so a world switch no longer has to flush the previous VM's TLB entries, because the MMU matches both the virtual address and the VM identifier against each entry. I/O support was added (multiqueue devices, better interrupt routing).

front: x86 virtualization: what do Intel's VT-x, VT-d, and IOV/VMDq brand?
back:
• VT-x (CPU): fix the instructions, extended page tables
  • VT-d (chipset): I/O routing, direct device access
  • IOV / VMDq (device-resident): DMA remapping, per-VM queues

front: x86 virtualization: how does the hardware fix relate to Popek & Goldberg's Theorem 1?
back: Forcing the 17 sensitive-but-unprivileged instructions to trap makes x86 satisfy Theorem 1. Once they trap they join the privileged set, so the sensitive set becomes a subset of the privileged set, and the trap-and-emulate VMM the paper proves constructible can be built directly in hardware rather than worked around in software.

front: x86 virtualization: what did Rosenblum & Garfinkel predict in 2005 about hardware support?
back: They noted Vanderpool and Pacifica had announced support that, rather than making existing modes virtualizable, adds a new execution mode so a VMM can use direct execution safely, cutting both the number and cost of traps. They forecast that adequate hardware support would make a fully compatible VM abstraction outweigh the performance benefit of breaking compatibility, that is, outweigh paravirtualization.

front: Memory virtualization (full): what three address types are distinguished, and what two page tables result?
back:
• Virtual: used by guest applications
  • Physical: used by the guest kernel, which still sees a contiguous linear space starting at 0
  • Machine: the real physical addresses of the platform
The guest OS maps virtual to physical; the hypervisor maps physical to machine. The first translation is pure software, and only the second can leverage the MMU and TLB, which adds overhead on every memory reference.

front: Memory virtualization (full): what is a shadow page table, and what must the hypervisor do to keep it consistent?
back: The hypervisor maps virtual addresses directly to machine addresses, skipping physical. To keep it consistent with the guest's table it invalidates the shadow page table on context switch and write-protects the guest page table, so every new guest mapping traps into the hypervisor, which then updates the shadow table.

front: Memory virtualization (paravirtualized): how does the guest handle page tables, and how is the trap cost reduced?
back: The guest need not use contiguous physical memory from 0; it registers its page tables with the hypervisor, so there is no second page table. The guest still lacks write permission to that table (now used directly by hardware), so every write traps to the hypervisor; the modified guest batches page table updates into a single hypercall, amortizing the VM exit cost.

front: Device virtualization: why are devices the hard case compared to CPU and memory?
back: CPU/memory virtualization is eased by strong standardization at the instruction set architecture level: for a given ISA the VMM supports one well-defined instruction set and ignores lower-level differences. Devices have no such standardization, there is enormous diversity in device types and interface semantics. Solutions pick one of three models.

front: Device virtualization: how does the passthrough (VMM-bypass) model work, and its weaknesses?
back: The VMM-level driver sets access permissions once (maps the device's registers into the guest), then steps aside; the guest's own driver drives the device directly. Strength: the VMM is out of the data path. Weaknesses: exclusive access makes sharing hard (VMM must keep reassigning the device), and the guest needs the exact device type present, which re-couples guest and hardware and makes migration hard (device-resident state must be copied).

front: Device virtualization: how does the hypervisor-direct model work, and its weaknesses?
back: The VMM intercepts every device request, translates it to a generic I/O operation for that device family, and runs it down the hypervisor-resident I/O stack to the real driver. Strengths: the guest stays decoupled from hardware (migration stays easy) and device sharing works. Weaknesses: emulation adds latency on every access, and the hypervisor must support all the drivers, inheriting their complexity. Originally adopted by VMware ESX; vendors provide drivers for its hypervisor, which sustained the model.

front: Device virtualization: how does the split device driver model work, and its one key limitation?
back: Two cooperating parts: a front-end driver in the guest VM and a back-end driver in the service VM (type 1) or host OS (type 2). The front end wraps guest device operations in special messages passed directly to the back-end component, which issues the real requests. The front-end driver looks like a wrapper for the device API, so guest applications are unmodified. It eliminates device emulation overhead (the layer need not reverse-engineer what the guest is trying to do) and the centralized back end manages shared devices well, but the front end must be modified, so it works only for paravirtualized guests. The back-end driver itself is usually unmodified.

front: Device virtualization: the through-line contrast across passthrough, hypervisor-direct, and split device?
back: Passthrough: the VMM is out of the data path, at the cost of device sharing and of decoupling (exact device type needed, migration hard). Hypervisor-direct: keeps decoupling and sharing, at the cost of emulation latency on every access and hypervisor driver complexity. Split device: eliminates emulation overhead and manages shared devices through a centralized back end, at the cost of a modified front end, so only paravirtualized guests.

front: Device virtualization: how does Rosenblum & Garfinkel frame device I/O historically, and what three approaches map onto the three models?
back: Thirty years earlier IBM mainframes used a channel-based I/O architecture, with a separate channel processor letting the VMM export device access directly to the VM at very low overhead. x86 lost that, and its huge, diverse device collection makes a VMM I/O layer a large effort. The three approaches only partly line up with the three models: the hosted architecture routes I/O through the host's drivers (highest overhead, VMware Workstation); ESX Server borrows Linux drivers directly (lower overhead; this is the hypervisor-direct model); and VMware exports optimized paravirtualized virtual devices needing a special guest driver (the split-device idea).

front: RPC: what is the motivation?
back: Almost every client/server program repeats the same low-level plumbing: with a socket API the developer must create and initialize sockets, allocate buffers, populate them with protocol information (such as a "get file" directive and the buffer size), and explicitly copy data in and out. Two apps may differ only in request name and payload yet need nearly identical setup. RPC lets a programmer call a remote procedure as if it were local, focusing on what the service does rather than the transport.

front: RPC: what three things does it concretely provide?
back:
• A high-level interface for data movement and communication (write add(i, j) instead of socket code)
  • Built-in handling of many low-level communication/transmission errors, so each program need not re-implement error handling
  • Hides the complexities of cross-machine interactions

front: RPC: what was Birrell and Nelson's guiding principle, and what consequence did it have for timeouts?
back: The semantics of remote procedure calls should be as close as possible to those of local procedure calls. They follow it even where distributed-systems practice would differ: the paper provides no time-out limiting a call's duration in the absence of machine or communication failures, because local calls have none.

front: RPC design point, binding/registry: contrast the two registry extremes.
back: At one extreme, a distributed online platform where any RPC service can register. At the other, a per-machine registry: a dedicated process on every server machine that knows only that machine's processes; clients must then already know the host's machine address, and the registry need only provide the service's port number.

front: RPC design point, failure semantics: why can the runtime usually not say what failed?
back: Many independent things can fail (lost client packet, lost server packet, downed network link, downed server machine, failed server process, overloaded server process), and several could happen at once. From a timeout alone the runtime can conclude only that the cause is any of the above; it cannot single one out. A single catch-all failure is honest but uninformative.

front: RPC design point, interface specification: language-agnostic vs. language-specific IDL tradeoffs?
back: A language-specific IDL (e.g. Java RMI uses Java) is natural if you already know that language and avoids learning a new notation. A language-agnostic IDL (e.g. XDR) lets a C client talk to a server written in anything, at the cost of learning the IDL; for programmers who do not know the server's language, learning a language-agnostic IDL is simpler than learning a whole new programming language.

front: RPC design point, pointer arguments: the two options and their tradeoff?
back: Disallow pointers as arguments to any RPC procedure. Or allow them, marshaling the referenced data (not the pointer) into the transmitted buffer; on the server the unmarshalling code passes the address of the unpacked data to the local procedure, so pointers are "passed".

front: RPC call-semantics spectrum: define at-least-once, at-most-once, and exactly-once-on-return.
back:
• At-least-once: blindly retransmit the whole call until a reply arrives; fine for idempotent procedures, dangerous for non-idempotent procedures
  • At-most-once: remember a call id so the callee discards duplicates (some degree of at-most-once)
  • Exactly-once (on return): (Paper, Birrell & Nelson: the packet protocol pairs retransmission with call identifiers and a per-activity sequence number; if the call returns, it was invoked exactly once; if an exception is reported, it was invoked once or not at all, and the user is not told which)

front: RPC: lecture presents binding as distributed vs. per-machine registry. What does Birrell and Nelson's paper actually use?
back: The paper's binding uses Grapevine, a replicated distributed database, binding an importer to an exporter by interface type and instance. The per-machine registry is the SunRPC point in the space, not the paper's.

front: SunRPC: what is it, and what binding/registry choice does it make?
back: SunRPC is the RPC package Sun built in the 1980s for NFS on UNIX, now widely ported. Binding is per-machine: a registry daemon called portmapper runs on every machine (TCP and UDP port 111). The server registers its service with the local portmapper on startup; the client contacts the portmapper on the target machine to obtain the port. rpcinfo -p lists the program id, version, protocol, port, and name of every registered service.

front: SunRPC: what interface-specification choice does it make, and what does rpcgen produce?
back: Language-agnostic: SunRPC uses XDR both to specify the interface and to encode each data type on the wire. The interface lives in a .x file; rpcgen -C <interface>.x compiles it into <interface>.h (types/prototypes), <interface>_svc.c (server stub plus a main with registration), <interface>_clnt.c (client stub), and <interface>_xdr.c (marshaling routines shared by both sides).

front: SunRPC: what failure semantics does it provide, and how does that compare to the paper?
back: SunRPC exposes error codes and tries to return a meaningful error as often as possible. It includes a configurable retry mechanism for re-contacting a server after a timeout. The number of retries can be specified (a bounded number); blind retransmission of the whole call gives only at-least-once semantics, unsafe for non-idempotent procedures, a different point from the paper's exactly-once-on-return. ONC RPC (RFC 1831): over an unreliable transport a reply implies at-least-once, a remembered transaction id can give some degree of at-most-once, and only a reliable transport yields exactly-once.

front: SunRPC: how does it handle pointers, binding handles, and threading?
back:
• Pointers: allowed; it serializes the pointed-to data, and server-side unmarshalling hands the local procedure the address of the reconstructed data
