  • Binding handle: clnt_create(host, prog, vers, proto) returns a CLIENT* used on every call to track per-client RPC state, status, errors, and authentication
  • Threading: rpcgen output is not thread-safe by default; -M makes it thread-safe, -A generates a multithreaded server on Solaris (on Linux it must be written by hand)

front: RPC: define marshaling and unmarshalling.
back: Marshaling: collecting arguments from scattered, non-contiguous locations in the caller's address space and packing them, with a descriptor of which procedure to invoke, into a single contiguous buffer; needed because a socket sends a contiguous byte stream, not program variables. Unmarshalling: the inverse on the receiver, extracting the correct byte ranges and using them to allocate and initialize the corresponding data structures in the callee's address space.

front: RPC: why are marshaling routines not hand-written, and why must both ends agree on a format?
back: The routines are generated by an IDL compiler from the interface specification and linked in. Marshaling also encodes data into an agreed format so the receiver can interpret it regardless of endianness or native representation; both ends must agree on the convention in advance or the receiver cannot recover the structure.

front: RPC: the two conventions for serializing a variable-size structure such as an array?
back:
• Write the length first, then the elements (length-prefixed), or
  • Write the elements followed by a terminator (the convention strings use, where the null byte marks the end)
The receiver, knowing the convention, reads the length (or scans to the terminator), allocates the right amount of memory, and copies the bytes in.

front: XDR: name the base types, including hyper, quadruple, const, and opaque (note the lecture vs. standard discrepancy).
back: Base types include char, byte, int, float; hyper is a 64-bit integer; quadruple is a 128-bit float (the lecture calls it 120-bit; XDR per RFC 4506 and Sun/Oracle define it as 128 bits / 16 bytes). const compiles to a C #define. opaque is uninterpreted binary data (e.g. image bytes).

front: XDR: how is a variable-length array (int data<80>) compiled and processed?
back: It compiles to a struct with two fields: an integer len holding the actual element count and a pointer val to the elements. The sender sets len and points val at the data; the receiver reads the first four bytes to learn len, allocates that much memory, and copies the rest in. A fixed-length array is written int data[80].

front: XDR: compute the in-memory size of a full variable-length int array of max size 5 on a 32-bit machine.
back: 4-byte len + 4-byte val pointer + five 4-byte ints = 28 bytes.

front: XDR: how are strings represented, and why is that an exception?
back: Other variable-length arrays compile to a len/val struct in memory. Strings do not: in memory they are stored as normal null-terminated strings, and only when encoded for transmission are they stored as a pair of len and data.

front: RPC: what is the sole reference paper for P4L1, and the names of its stub generator and registry?
back: The reference is Birrell and Nelson, "Implementing Remote Procedure Calls". Its stub generator is named Lupine and its registry is Grapevine.

front: Distributed service: contrast the upload/download and true-remote-access extremes.
back: Upload/download: the client downloads the whole file, modifies locally, uploads it back; modifications are fast with no per-operation network cost, but it transfers the entire file even for small modifications and the server loses control while it is checked out. True remote access: the file stays on the server and every operation crosses the network; the server keeps full control and consistency is easy, but every operation pays a network cost and the server saturates quickly, limiting scalability.

front: Distributed service: what is the practical compromise between the two extremes, and its cost?
back: Let clients cache blocks (and prefetch likely-next blocks). This cuts latency and server load, but forces clients to tell the server about modifications and to check whether cached blocks have been invalidated by others, which makes the server more complex and introduces non-UNIX sharing semantics the client must understand.

front: Distributed service: stateless vs. stateful on failure recovery and caching?
back: Stateless: keeps no client/file/access state; failure recovery is trivial (just restart; clients reissue timed-out requests and get the same answers); caching with consistency is not possible (no state to drive coherence). Stateful: knows which files/blocks are open, by whom, read vs. write, who cached what; caching plus locking are supported; failure recovery is hard (state must be recovered, so it must be checkpointed to be rebuilt). Any caching model needs a stateful server.

front: Distributed service: stateless vs. stateful on request form and bits on the wire?
back: Stateless: every request is self-contained (absolute offsets, all parameters), so more bits per request. Stateful: can use relative requests ("next kB of data"), so fewer bits on the wire, at the cost of runtime overhead to maintain state and run coherence protocols.

front: Distributed service, caching: what does client-side caching buy, and what does it cost?
back: It lets repeated reads hit local memory/disk, lowering latency and server load. The cost is cache coherence: when one client writes a block another has cached, the system needs a mechanism (on-demand, periodic, or on-open; client- or server-driven) to propagate or invalidate. Coherence requires server state, so caching and statelessness are incompatible.

front: Distributed service, replication: what is it, its benefits, and its costs?
back: Every server holds all files. Benefits: requests can be load balanced across replicas (better performance), the system is more available, and it is more fault tolerant (when one replica fails, the others serve clients with no degradation). Costs: writes become complex (write synchronously to all replicas, or write one and asynchronously propagate), replicas can diverge and must be reconciled (e.g. majority voting), and it does not scale in capacity (adding a machine does not let you store more files).

front: Distributed service, partitioning: what is it, its benefits, and its costs?
back: Each server holds a disjoint subset of files (by filename, by directory (partitioning the hierarchical namespace), or by other criteria). Benefits: scales in capacity (more machines means more files), and writes are simple (a file lives on exactly one machine). Costs: when a partition fails its files are unavailable, load balancing must account for access skew, and a heavily-accessed file creates a hotspot. A common combination partitions across one axis then replicates each partition.

front: Distributed service: contrast session semantics and periodic updates as update strategies.
back: Session semantics: write back on close, check for a newer version on open; easy to reason about but poor for concurrent sharing and allow long staleness windows. Periodic updates: client flushes periodically, server sends periodic invalidations; this bounds inconsistency in time. Other strategies: immutable files (never modify; create a new file) and transactions (batch updates applied atomically).

front: Sprite: what is the reference paper for P4L2?
back: Nelson, Welch, and Ousterhout, "Caching in the Sprite Network File System".

front: Sprite: observation "about one-third of accesses are writes" drove what design decision?
back: Caching is worthwhile for the two-thirds of reads, but a write-through cache cannot reduce disk or server traffic by more than two-thirds, so write-through alone is insufficient. Use a delayed write-back policy.

front: Sprite: observation "20-30% of new data deleted within 30 s, 50% within 5 min" drove what design decision?
back: Delayed write-back pays off: data deleted before it is written back never needs to be written at all.

front: Sprite: observation "75% of files open < 0.5 s, 90% < 10 s" drove what design decision?
back: Files are open so briefly that the overheads of session semantics (write-back on close) are still too high; the paper rejects write-on-close with these open-duration numbers.

front: Sprite: observation "concurrent write-sharing is rare" drove what design decision?
back: Optimize the consistency algorithm for the no-sharing case; disable caching entirely during concurrent write-sharing, since the cost is paid infrequently.

front: Sprite: summarize the resulting caching policy.
back: Client caching (Paper, Nelson et al.: main-memory caches on both clients and servers); delayed write-back where every 30 seconds all dirty blocks not modified in the last 30 seconds are written back; every open goes to the server (so directories/names are not cached); and caching disabled for a file while it is concurrently write-shared, with all its accesses serialized at the server.

front: Sprite: the lecture says the statistics come from Sprite's own production filesystem and that the 30-second interval was derived from the deletion figure. What does the paper actually say?
back: The write %, open-duration, and deletion numbers come from the earlier BSD study, a trace of three time-shared VAX-11/780s running 4.2 BSD UNIX; Sprite reuses that trace in a simulation (Tables 1 and 2) and again in Section 7 to size a Sprite server. The one-third write figure is used as an upper bound ("write-through cannot reduce traffic by more than two-thirds"), not a count of improvable operations. The 30-second interval is the UNIX convention (the 30-second sync interval), not tuned to the deletion statistic; the paper notes the trace actually argues for a longer delay.

front: Sprite: what is the paper's own evidence on write-sharing frequency (vs. the lecture's "concurrent write-sharing rare")?
back: "Concurrent write-sharing rare" is the paper's expectation about Sprite's own sharing, used to justify optimizing for the no-sharing case, not a BSD-trace measurement. The paper's own sharing evidence is its Section 5.3 simulation: of all write traffic, 4041 blocks were written through for concurrent write-sharing and 6887 flushed for sequential write-sharing, and consistency accounted for about one-fourth of server traffic.

front: Sprite: what per-file state does the client keep?
back:
• cache (overall cacheable yes/no for this file)
  • the set of cached blocks
  • a timer/timestamp per dirty block (to drive the 30-second write-back)
  • a version number

front: Sprite: what per-file state does the server keep?
back:
• the set of readers
  • the current writer
  • a version number
Separately, to enable/disable caching during concurrent sharing, the server also keeps a per-file cacheable flag.

front: Sprite: how do version numbers solve the first sequential-write-sharing problem?
back: (Paper, Nelson et al.: the problem is that the opener's own cache may be stale. The server increments the version each time the file is opened for writing; a client compares its stored version against the server's on open and flushes its cached copy if they differ.)

front: Sprite: how does last-writer tracking solve the second sequential-write-sharing problem?
back: (Paper, Nelson et al.: the problem is that current data may still sit in the previous writer's cache (the last writer need not have flushed on close). On a new open by a different client, the server tells the last writer to flush its dirty blocks through before the opener reads.)

front: Sprite: what does the server do on concurrent write-sharing?
back: (Paper, Nelson et al.: on concurrent write-sharing (file open on multiple clients with at least one writer), the server (1) tells the single writer, if any, to write back all dirty blocks (there can be at most one), and (2) tells all clients currently holding the file open that it is no longer cacheable, so they drop its blocks and go to the server; all operations then go through the server. Clients holding stale blocks but not currently open are not notified; they act at their next open.)

front: Sprite: lecture says "when the writer closes, the server makes the file cacheable again." What is the paper's narrower rule?
back: Disabling is per file and only while sharing is concurrent; for simplicity Sprite does not re-enable caching for a file that is still open once it becomes cacheable again. This contradicts the lecture's scenario: the remaining writer still has the file open, so under the paper it would not resume caching until it closes and reopens the file; caching is re-enabled only for later opens.

front: DSM: what is the uniform tension in choosing sharing granularity?
back: Finer granularity generates coherence traffic too often to be affordable over a network; coarser granularity amortizes network cost over a larger unit but risks false sharing.

front: DSM granularity: why are cache-line and variable granularity unsuitable for DSM?
back: Cache line is the SMP hardware unit, but far too fine for DSM: generating coherence traffic per cache line is too expensive, because that traffic must travel over the network. Variable granularity is meaningful to the programmer but still too fine; many variables are only a few bytes long, so coherence overhead over the network stays too high.

front: DSM granularity: the for/against of page and object granularity?
back: Page: natural to the OS (no language support needed) and large enough to amortize remote-access cost, but must beware false sharing (two nodes writing different variables on the same page trigger logically unnecessary coherence traffic). Object: no OS modification needed (the OS knows nothing about objects), but requires a language runtime that understands local vs. remote objects, so it is not generalizable across languages. With a cooperating compiler, objects can be laid out on separate pages to use a page-based OS mechanism without the language dependency.

front: DSM granularity: how does Protic et al. frame the tradeoff, and what two adverse effects of coarse grain does it name?
back: The paper frames granularity as a two-sided tradeoff: coarser blocks save directory storage and suit high-locality applications but raise the chance that different processors contend for the same block even when touching unrelated parts. It names false sharing together with thrashing as the two adverse effects of coarse-grain, virtual-memory-based software DSM.

front: DSM indexing: what metadata locates a page's manager and keeps the page consistent, and where does each piece live?
back:
1. Locating the manager: each page's address (node id + page frame number) identifies its home node (manager); a global map from page id to manager id is replicated on every node
  2. Keeping it consistent: each manager maintains the per-page metadata needed to perform accesses to that page or force its consistency, so this metadata is partitioned across the system

front: DSM: why split a replicated global index from partitioned per-page local indices?
back: A small global map (page/object id to manager id) is replicated on every node, so any node can find the manager of any page. The per-page (local) metadata is partitioned across the system, so no single node holds all of it; each manager keeps the metadata only for its own pages.

front: DSM: why distinguish a home node from an owner node?
back: When a non-home node accesses a page repeatedly or exclusively, continually routing updates through the home node is expensive. Ownership (the right to drive coherence and modify) can migrate to that node, and the home node's role narrows to tracking who the current owner is. The address itself is a (node id, page frame number) pair; the mapping table lets the manager node change without changing the object identifier, while the home node tracks the current owner.

front: DSM: what per-page metadata does the home node typically keep?
back: Pages accessed, and by whom (readers, writers), modifications, caching enabled/disabled, and lock status. Separately, replicas can be created deliberately for load balancing, hot spot avoidance, or reliability (e.g. triplicating state on the original machine, a nearby machine in the same rack, and a remote machine in another rack or another datacenter).

front: DSM implementation: what is the central lever, and how are remote reads detected?
back: The lever is the MMU: intervene only on accesses that touch shared state, stay out of the way otherwise. A reference to a remote address has no valid local page-table mapping, so the hardware traps into the OS, which passes the access information to the DSM layer to send out the appropriate remote message.

front: DSM implementation: how are writes to shared state detected and handled?
back: When content is cached on a node, the DSM layer write-protects that memory. A write attempt traps into the OS, which passes the relevant information to the DSM layer to generate the necessary coherence messages. The page's home node (or current owner) drives the coherence operations for that page.

front: DSM implementation: what is the benefit of using faults, and what extra MMU information is useful?
back: Using faults means the DSM machinery is invoked only on shared-state access; purely local accesses proceed with no overhead (dynamic engage/disengage). Extra MMU information: dirty and accessed bits can be read to implement different consistency policies. For object-granularity DSM the same ideas move into a language runtime.

front: Consistency model: what is it, and what two questions does it answer?
back: A consistency model is a guarantee the DSM layer makes about how memory updates become visible, contingent on the software following a set of rules. It answers: in what order are operations observed, and how recent is the value a reader sees.

front: Consistency: define strict consistency and why it is impractical.
back: Strict consistency: every read returns the value of the most recent write, with "most recent" fixed by absolute global time; all nodes see all writes in the same order, immediately. It requires instantaneous, globally-ordered visibility and is impossible in practice; even a single SMP gives no such guarantee across cores without extra synchronization, and distributed latency/loss/reordering rule it out. A theoretical ideal only.

front: Consistency: state the two rules of sequential consistency.
back: Visibility need not be immediate, but the observed order must correspond to some legal interleaving, subject to: (1) operations issued by a single process appear in all observers in that process's issue order; (2) all processes observe the same single interleaving.

front: Consistency: P1 writes x to m1 and P2, independently, writes y to m2. Can P3 see x at m1 then y at m2? Can it see 0 at m1 then y at m2?
back: Both are OK. The two writes are unrelated (P2 computed y without reference to m1), and each observation equals some possible ordering on a single shared-memory system. Sequential consistency instead forbids two processes observing different orders of the same updates (P3 sees m1 become x before m2 becomes y while P4 sees m2 as y with m1 still 0), and requires same-process operations to appear in issue order (e.g. if P1 later writes z to m3, no process may see z at m3 and only afterwards learn x was written to m1).

front: Consistency: define causal consistency.
back: Only potentially causally related writes must be seen in the same order by all processes; concurrent (causally unrelated) writes may be observed in different orders by different processes. A write that follows a read on the same process is treated as potentially dependent on the value read.

front: Consistency: causal-consistency example. P1 does W(m1)X; P2 does R(m1)X then W(m2)Y. What is forced?
back: Because Y may depend on X, a causally consistent system forces every other process to read X at m1 before it may read Y at m2. If instead W(m1)X and W(m2)Y were concurrent with no intervening read linking them, observers may see them in either order. Writes from the same process are still seen everywhere in issue order.

front: Consistency: define weak consistency and the role of sync.
back: Memory is guaranteed consistent only at explicit synchronization points (Protic et al.'s phrasing). The layer exports a sync operation. A process that made updates calls sync (an exit/release) to push them out; a process wanting others' updates calls sync (an entry/acquire) to pull them in. A sync by the writer alone does not make its writes visible to a reader that has not synchronized; both sides must participate. Once P2 syncs, it is guaranteed to see every update that existed as of P1's sync.

front: Consistency: weak-consistency example. P1 does W(m1)X then sync; is P2 guaranteed to see X?
back: Not at that moment, because P2 has not synchronized. After P2 performs its own sync, it is guaranteed to see X (and all other updates that preceded P1's sync).

front: Consistency: which of strict, sequential, causal, weak are in Protic et al.'s taxonomy, and where do the others come from?
back: Only sequential and weak are in Protic et al.'s taxonomy (sequential, processor, weak, release, lazy release, entry). Strict and causal are not in Protic; the lecture takes them from the general distributed-systems literature (Tanenbaum).

front: Consistency: what is processor consistency (which the lecture skips)?
back: (Paper, Protic et al.: a model between sequential and weak: all processors must observe the writes of any one processor in that processor's issue order, but need not agree on the interleaving of writes from different processors, and reads are allowed to bypass writes in the service queue. Examples: VAX 8800, Plus, Merlin, RMS.)

front: Consistency: how does the paper's finer taxonomy refine the lecture's single acquire/release weak-consistency mechanism?
back: The lecture's single acquire/release mechanism is, in the paper, release consistency (acquire gates later ordinary accesses; release waits for prior ordinary accesses). Entry consistency is distinct and more aggressive: it additionally binds each shared variable to a specific synchronization variable, so an acquire propagates only the data that variable guards; the lecture's "entry/acquire" label does not fully capture it. Lazy release postpones propagation to the next relevant acquire, contrasted with "eager" release. The paper also requires the synchronization accesses themselves to be sequentially consistent.

front: Large-scale systems: in a homogeneous design, what can each worker node do, and what are the pros?
back: Every node can perform any step of request processing for any request type; data is replicated or distributed so any node can reach any information it needs. Pros: the front-end is simple (round-robin, optionally weighted by observed CPU load, with no knowledge of request content), and scaling is trivial (add or remove interchangeable nodes).

front: Large-scale systems: what is the main con of a homogeneous design?
back: Little benefit from caching or locality. A simple front-end keeps too little state to route by locality, so a given node sees a mix of unrelated work and its cache hit rate stays low.

front: Large-scale systems: in a heterogeneous design, how are nodes organized, and what are the pros?
back: Each node specializes in a subset of requests or processing steps (e.g. eBay routing browse requests to one pool and bid/buy to another, or splitting by alphabetical order of a requested filename). Pros: caching and locality pay off, because each node repeatedly works on similar data and computations, so useful data is more likely cached; data need not be uniformly accessible everywhere.

front: Large-scale systems: what are the cons of a heterogeneous design?
back: The front-end is more complex (it must parse requests to route them). Management is harder: scaling is no longer "add a node" (you must know which specialized pool is the bottleneck), idle nodes of the wrong type cannot absorb excess load, and workload shifts force layout reconfiguration. This makes hotspots and long per-node backlogs easier to fall into. The core tradeoff: simplicity and easy scaling vs. locality and cache efficiency at the cost of routing/management complexity.

front: Cloud: what imbalanced workload motivated AWS, and when did EC2 launch?
back: Amazon in the mid 2000s had an imbalanced workload: most traffic came during the US holiday shopping season (Thanksgiving to Christmas), so much hardware provisioned for that peak sat idle outside that window, or was used for other company tasks such as forecasting or other analytics. In 2006 Amazon opened its hardware to third-party workloads over web APIs for a fee, the birth of AWS and EC2.

front: Cloud: how does the Animoto example illustrate elasticity?
back: Animoto turned photos into videos (compute-heavy) and rented EC2 instances instead of building a datacenter. When it launched to Facebook users in April 2008 it signed up 750,000 users in three days and scaled from about 50 instances Monday to 400 Tuesday to 3,400 by Friday, roughly two orders of magnitude in a week, which owned infrastructure could not have met.

front: Cloud: what is the older utility-computing vision, and the summarized goals of cloud computing?
back: John McCarthy in 1961 envisioned computing organized as a public utility, like the telephone system. Cloud computing aims to turn IT resources into a fungible utility consumed without caring which hardware serves you. Goals: on-demand elastic resources, fine-grained usage-based pricing, professional hosting/management, and API-based access, so cost tracks demand instead of being fixed at peak-provisioning levels.

front: Cloud: what are the limits on the utility vision?
back: Hardware dependencies cannot be fully masked even with virtualization; providers expose different APIs (API lock-in); putting core code and data with a provider raises privacy/security concerns; and geographic distance adds latency.

front: Cloud service models: for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, what does the provider own, and give an example of each.
back:
• IaaS: provider owns physical hardware (and virtualization); customer brings applications, data, runtime, middleware, and O/S. Example: Amazon EC2
  • PaaS: provider owns hardware + infrastructure + execution environment (OS, tools); customer brings application and data. Example: Google App Engine; early Windows Azure (.NET)
  • SaaS: provider owns application, data, infrastructure, hardware; customer brings nothing. Example: Gmail

text: Cloud deployment models: {{c1::public}} is provider-owned and rented by tenants; {{c2::private}} has the same entity owning infrastructure and software in-house; {{c3::hybrid}} uses private for the main load with public for failover/spikes or auxiliary tasks like load testing; and {{c4::community}} is a public cloud shared by a particular class of users.

front: Cloud: name the enabling technologies that make cloud offerings broadly useful.
back:
• Virtualization: makes physical hardware into fungible resources
  • Resource provisioning and scheduling: dynamic provisioning and scheduling of infrastructure resources (Mesos, Hadoop's YARN)
  • Big-data processing (e.g. Hadoop MapReduce, Spark)
  • Data storage: append-only distributed filesystems; NoSQL databases; storing data across distributed memories instead of repeatedly accessing disk
  • Isolation: software that can enable and configure software-defined slices of resources (each customer gets its own software-defined data center)
  • Monitoring (e.g. Flume, CloudWatch, Log Insight)

front: Cloud: from the provider's side, what two things make the cloud practical at scale?
back:
• Law of large numbers: averaged across many clients whose peaks are shifted in time, aggregate demand is roughly constant, so a fixed amount of hardware serves many clients without any one peak consuming everything
  • Economies of scale: the fixed cost of hardware is amortized across many tenants; more clients means lower per-client cost

front: Cloud: from the client's side, what makes the cloud practical at scale?
back: Elasticity of resources and of cost: capacity scales elastically with demand, ideally instantaneously and automatically, with the provisioned resources accessible anywhere, anytime, so the cost of the service is directly proportional to demand. Owned infrastructure is either over-provisioned (paying for idle capacity) or maxed out (dropping requests). For this the cloud must provide fungible resources, dynamic resource management at very large scale, performance isolation across multi-tenant environments, and guarantees of the privacy of client data and the security of the execution environment.

front: Cloud: give the formula for the probability that at least one of n independent components fails, and the worked values for p=0.03.
back: P(at least one failure) = 1 - (1 - p)^n. With p = 0.03: n = 10 gives about 26%; n = 100 gives about 95%.

front: Cloud: why are failures unavoidable at scale, and what mechanisms must the system incorporate?
back: Real cloud systems have thousands or hundreds of thousands of components, so even with more reliable hardware, something somewhere will be failing. The system must incorporate failure handling: timeouts for detection, restart and retry for recovery, and backup, replication, and checkpointing.
